difficult and tough economic times that we have had to go through, is one of the reasons
why New Zealanders voted in large numbers for National, and I think we are very lucky
that New Zealanders actually think with that perspective.
In the next 3 years, this Government  is focused on making our country more
competitive so that it can fulfil more of our  potential as a nation, and we want to keep
our promise to New Zealanders. One of the ways that we are doing that is by way of
improving the welfare system, and spe nding $8 billion and having 351,000 people on
the benefit is not the way to go.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: There are times when you wait
in this debate for an enlightened contribu tion, but unfortunately that was not one of
them. Did we hear about the per capita GDP  of Finland? Oh, no—cannot mention those
facts. Or the total GDP per capita compared with Finland’s? No comment about that. Or
the take-home pay of the Finnish people co mpared with New Zealand’s? No, that
member could not mention that because th at is a comparison that National members
cannot even stand up against.
But our Government has a Cabinet Manual. Clearly Merrill Lynch never did. And all
over New Zealand there was a huge sigh from  local government at 2 o’clock this
afternoon. There was a massive sigh from lo cal government all around this country. But
if the Prime Minister and Nick Smith thi nk that they have dodged the bullets over the
ACC dispute or debate, then we have got ne ws for them, and it is all bad. We want to
know the facts behind this.

items.speaker: We remember that John Key said
items.text: “I expect  high standards from my Ministers.” If
those are high standards, then you could para chute them out the backside of a rabbit.
That is what you could do with them. He sa id: ‘I expect high standards.” That was his
boast. If any member of Parliament from anothe r party had written as a Minister a letter
on ministerial letterhead like this, National members would be screaming for blood. But
there they sit, all mute, on the backbench, hoping: “Well, Nick’s gone; maybe they will
put me there.” You can see the egregious, self -centred concern they have, not for Nick.
They remind me of the Highveld in Africa,  where there are a w hole lot of animals
grazing there, and out of th e long grass comes this lion. And they all run like nobody’s
business to get out of the way. But as soon as the lion gets the first one, they all stop and
start grazing. That is the National Party. That is the National Party. They emulate and
resemble nature.
The Prime Minister, Mr Key, knew about th is case. My question is: when did he
know and how much did he know? That is wh ere this issue is going now. He can think
he can hide behind the second letter, pu lled out from 2010 as being the second
unforgivable sin—not the one ju st last year. The unforgiva ble one was the one in 2010,
which we did not know about. We want to see all the emails, all the texts, between Miss
Pullar and Nick Smith.
Su’a William Sio: Were there any photographs?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, there may be photographs. I am not pushing it
too far, because we are going from what we know, and we are not going to speculate on
what we do not know.
Let me make it very, very clear. What did the Prime Minister do  about it when he
knew? He knew, for example, that Miss Pullar was putting pre ssure on Nick Smith.
What did he do about it? Apparently, nothing.  Did he advise Nick Smith as to what
should be done? Did he advise any of hi s other colleagues? He knew what was going
21 Mar 2012 General Debate 1167
on. Take former party president, Michelle Boag. Why was she involved? Why was this
woman involved? She is someone  who got lined up at court for trying to pervert the
course of justice—do you remember—in a massive commission of inquiry. And she got
fined for it. Nothing—no problem for the Nati onal Party. Talk about standards! They
have not got any.
Today we learnt about the second error,  the letter of 2010. You know something?
This is not going to be a Pansy Wong situation, where she jumped ship and said: “Look,
I’m resigning. I’m coming home, Sammy.” Oh, no. We know that there was a lot
behind the Pansy Wong story, which goes al l the way to a former National Prime
Minister—and they know as well. The problem with this Government is it did not press
on and it should have. In this case, we are. We are going to find out what it knew, when
it knew, and what it did not do about it when it should have acted.
Why did the Prime Minister not instruct his Minister to tell Miss Pullar to go and get
help somewhere else? Why did he not do that ? The issue is not a case for the Privacy
Commissioner—[Interruption] Pardon?

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: We want to know.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Because he thought he could slide by and none of us
would know. But unfortunately this is a sm all country, and the National members are
now finding out again what they should have acted on when they first knew.
It is not a case for the Privacy Commissioner any more. This goes to the quality and
transparency of Government.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Gloating, as the Hon Tau Henare
has noted, is never an attractive option, yet despite some pretty cute attempts from some
of the speakers opposite today, that is exactly what they have been doing. It began with
Grant Robertson, it continued with Chris Hipkins, it became  particularly odious under
David Cunliffe, and now we have just had it from the 35 th member of the Labour Party
caucus, Winston Peters. Revelling in another’ s misfortune, when that person has acted
honourably—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is not a debatable
issue, because we had an election. There is no 35th member of the Labour Party caucus.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: There’s a proud party called New Zealand First.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No—that is not a point of
order.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I am pleased to advise the
member that apparently not even the Labour Party caucus wants him, either. But I want
to say that revelling in another’s misfortune, when that person has acted honourably—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This member has been in
the Parliament now for, I think—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: 3 years.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Three years? Sorry, I thought  he was new—a number of
months, anyway. He should know by now, Mr Assistant Speaker, th at he must not
comment on your very wise rulings.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That is perfectly correct, Mr
Mallard. I was actually thinking of frivolous interjections, but you are right.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I think Mr Mallard is well
aware of what he was attempting to do there, and I think it is unfortunate that he wanted
to interrupt me when I was making the point  about the courage of  the Minister, who,
unfortunately, has resigned today. I simply want to say that I am very proud to be—
1168 General Debate 21 Mar 2012

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member cannot
refer to the courage of members. It can be  seen as a personal reflection under Standing
Order 117.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: The Minister has acted with di gnity, and I am very proud to be
his colleague. I send my best wishes to Nick and his family at this time.
I am also proud to be a member of a very  busy, focused, and effective Government.
New Zealanders’ enthusiasm for our Labour opponents’ policies is currently about as
warm as the climate in Mr Shearer’s bel oved Finland at this time of the year.
Understandably, given the overwhelming rejection Labour received from New
Zealanders just a few months ago, it is now licking its wounds  and wondering how it
can reconnect with the electo rate. Well, nothing Labour members have said or done to
date, and certainly not in today’s general debate, indicates that they have a clue.
Yesterday during question time we heard from the member for Rimutaka, who
enjoyed his own contribution in inverse proportion to the rest of his audience. We heard
an attempt to ridicule this Government and our Ministers—wait for it—for having a
series of plans. “Far too many plans”, he spluttered.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: No, he didn’t.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Yes, he did, Ms King. He read out a whole lot of plans and
strategies, yet this was the same Mr Hipki ns who, along with his colleagues, half of
whom are now pursuing other career opport unities, repeatedly bleated during the
previous 3 years: “Where’s the plan? The Government hasn’t got a plan.” And every
time they were told the plan they feigned an  inability to understand it. Well, perhaps
they were not feigning it.
They are leaderless and directionless, an d their demeanour indicates, as do their
statements, that they are hopeless. In star k contrast, the National-led Government is
forging ahead with a visionary and appropria te programme to steer our country through
very difficult times. We have a widely resp ected Prime Minister, a talented and united
ministry, and a busy caucus blending industr y and experience with a superb group of
new MPs, who demonstrate that the National Pa rty is in excellent shape and clearly is
the right team in the right place at the right time. I want to congratulate my new caucus
colleagues—one of whom, Ms Barry, is sitti ng just in front of me—on their superb
maiden speeches, delivered in this House just a few weeks ago.
There is strong support in the Hamilton West electorate for the Government’s
determination to rein in Government sp ending; encourage appropriate investment;
deliver better, sooner, and more convenient h ealth-care; facilitate economic growth; lift
educational achievements for those who are struggling; and implement important
reforms to deliver better local government and to get our economy into surplus. These
are the issues that matter to New Zealand. Th ey are all areas where our Government is
making significant progress, notwithstanding the major problems we face—indeed,
most countries face—at the present time in each and every one of them.
In the remaining time I want to focu s on another major programme that we
campaigned on last year and that we will begin to implement this month. In our
previous term, despite vocal criticism from the depleted party opposite, the Government
implemented the highly successful Future Fo cus programme to begin rebalancing our
welfare system. The results to date have been very encouraging. Just by requiring
people to reapply for the unemployment bene fit after 1 year, so far 12,500 people have
cancelled their benefit. Of that number, mo re than half did not even complete the
application, and more than 3,300 of them had already found a job. As of last month,
year 1 Future Focus results included 10,400 fewer New Zealanders being on welfare,
while a further 2,300 people who were on the domestic purposes benefit—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Boring repetition.
21 Mar 2012 General Debate 1169

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: —took up part-time work. Mr Mallard finds all this boring.
Well, I think every one of these people will be delighted with those results, and we are
certainly proud of them as a Government. Thirteen thousand went off the domestic
purposes benefit into work, a nd 50 percent of beneficiarie s did not require a single
hardship benefit.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
SOUTHLAND DISTRICT COUNCIL (STEWART ISLAND/RAKIURA
VISITOR LEVY) EMPOWERING BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: ERIC ROY
items.text: I move, That the Southland District Council
(Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill be now read a third time . Can I
say at the outset that I wish to acknowledge my thanks to the House for allowing us to
move directly to the third r eading. It certainly was a prudent  thing to do given the time
this bill spent in the Local Government and Environment Committee and the fact that it
received unanimous support at its second reading.
But before I speak about the bill, I should acknowledge an event of some tragedy that
has overtaken the communities of Bluff, Ra kiura / Stewart Island, and Invercargill: the
sinking of the Easy Rider . This is the first opportunity I have had, and I inform the
House that tomorrow there will be a large funeral for the four people whose bodies have
been recovered. It will be held at Rugby Park Stadium in Southland and I will be
attending. I am sure the House would wish me to convey to all the friends and families
of the people who lost their lives our very best wishes. We understand their grief, we
feel some of their pain, and our prayers and thoughts are actu ally with them. I think we
would also want those families who do not ha ve their loved ones b ack to know that we
are thinking of them. I thi nk perhaps at this time we should also acknowledge Dallas
Reedy, the survivor. In the a nnals of human survival, 18 hour s in Foveaux Strait is a
feat that is rarely matched anywhere in the history of humankind. We just wish Dallas
well as he adjusts to actually surviving, a nd losing his mates, and finding a purpose for
his life from this point on. So I think the House should do that, and I will certainly take
the good wishes and our thoughts to the families and friends tomorrow.
This bill has certainly had an interesting passage and it is great to get to the third
reading. I think at earlier stages in the process of this bill I said that I first became aware
of the problem in 1994 when I was the member for Awarua. The pressures that visitors
created for the small community of Stewart Island was a significant issue. For a number
of years we had tried to put in place a vol untary scheme; for various reasons that was
not able to be achieved. A bi ll was drafted. It was sent b ack for further consultation, I
think twice, before we were able to table it and meet all the expectations and criteria set
out in the Standing Orders. The bill then received two extensions in the select
committee, as we worked through some issu es, which perturbed th e then Minister of
Local Government, the Hon Rodney Hide, an d probably perturbed his officials even
more. But we have come through that, and I f eel a little bit like uttering the comment
that Edmund Hillary related to John Hunt, after he had achieved a milestone on Everest.
However, I do know that that is probably unparliamentary.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I think so!

items.speaker: ERIC ROY
items.text: I think that comment will be used  more than once in the South Sea
Hotel in Oban after today, when I expect th at the House will agai n generously support
this Stewart Island visitor levy bill.
Can I also at this stage thank those members of the select committee. During the
course of this process I note that 18 people have been on the select committee and every
1170 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012
single one contributed to tryi ng to find solutions to those issues that needed some
resolution. I think sometimes members’ bills and local bills are when Parliament is seen
at its finest. There are no po litical divides. People genuinely try to find solutions, and at
the end of it there are small communities or  individuals, quite frequently, for whom we
do make a difference.
Stewart Island is one of those commun ities that, as I said, has been under a
significant amount of pressure . As we have gone through  the process here, members
have extolled the uniqueness and the beauty of Stewart Island. I think it is appropriate at
this third reading that I also  amplify a little bit about the pressures of living on Stewart
Island, in the way that their cost structure is just so much highe r than certainly all
mainland communities, and probably higher than many of the island communities
around New Zealand, as well. Of course there is the transport component in every single
thing that happens across one of the wildest stretches of water in the world, which we
have just referenced a little bit earlier. Ev en things like construction have a very high
cost. There is no really good quality aggregate on the island for building roads or
making concrete. So every single thing that is used on the island, virtually, has to be
transported on to it.
And add to that the difficulties of, for example, power generation where currently the
residents and consumers on St ewart Island are paying 58c a unit for power generation.
The last time I was on Stewart Island was a bout 4 weeks ago at a symposium that was
looking at the various options  from running a cable acro ss to Stewart Island to
hydroelectric, to wind, to wave, to current—j ust about every alternative that one could
imagine was analysed, and some direction was able to be found going forward.
On top of that, because of the high costs, the very nature of the community of
Stewart Island has changed. I did say at the out set that it is a community that has been
under some pressure. We have seen, for example, the fishing industry, which was one of
the bigger parts of the island in recent y ears, shift itself to Bluff for perhaps two
reasons. The first is the cost of processing on the island. The second is that for reasons
of sustainability some of  the quota management areas have been subdivided. For
example, in the pāua fishery it was very easy to sp end one’s time in and around Stewart
Island and deplete the areas immediately adjace nt. So that has been separated out, and
we have a more spread harvest, which has taken some of the activity away from Stewart
Island.
Currently, I guess, the two significant i ndustries on Stewart Is land are aquaculture,
where there is a large mussel producti on base, some salmon production, and, more
recently, farmed oysters as well. But the big earner and the big change in Stewart Island
has been catering to tourists, and, especi ally since the Rakiur a National Park was
established, this has gained some momentum. I think in an earlier speech I talked about
cruise ships. It was a rare thing a decade ago to see a cruise ship arrive at Stewart Island.
Last year in total there were  13 that visited the island. This  year, so far, I think the
number is 19 different cruise ships that have come.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: What do the islanders think of the pink shirt?

items.speaker: ERIC ROY
items.text: The islanders are people of impec cable taste and they love their MP.
Can I just say to any member who has any doubt  whatsoever that if they are on Stewart
Island, hospitality will be afforded to any memb er of this House who goes and says: “I
supported Eric’s levy bill.” And treats such as kina roe, blue cod, and all those
delicacies, which I have not yet spoken of, w ill be available to any member who uses
that secret password on Stewart Island.
It is just great that we have solved a bit of  an issue. One of the last points of concern
I would like to make has been that this bill mi ght set some sort of precedent. I guess in
answer to that, the House does set precedents in what it is doing, but I have made the
21 Mar 2012 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 1171
point in previous speeches in this House in relation to this  bill that the situation on
Stewart Island is so unique, with the very small population catering for tens of
thousands of people, that it is not likely that  the exact circumstances will be replicated.
People go to Stewart Island for all sorts of  reasons. There are trampers, fishers,
birdwatchers, or people who just want to get away and enjoy the serenity while there is
some very poor cellphone coverage, and they are able to just chill out. I just again thank
the House for its participation in this proce ss. I look forward to the conclusion of this
matter with the passing of the third reading. I thank all members for their efforts.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: This House does join with Eric Roy
in sending our condolences to the familie s of those who lost their life on the Easy Rider
last week. I thank the member for raising that matter today.
I want to start off by congratulating Eric  Roy on bringing the Southland District
Council (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill to the House. I think he
shows what a good local representative can do. In fact, I think he probably should be the
next Minister that comes into Cabinet, fo llowing the resignation of Nick Smith today.
Eric Roy has the experience a nd he has the integrity to ma ke a very good Minister, and
perhaps he will get that opportunity. But he is well known for supporting local
activities. Some members come into this H ouse wanting the title. Others come in to
work hard in their electorate, and I just want to say that Eric Roy is one of those.
But I do take exception to one thing that he said. He said this bill is very unique, for a
unique part of New Zealand. I am sure he has not forgotten that I represent a very
unique island group in New Zealand—the Ch atham Islands. I have been the member
there for 16 years. The Chatham Islands are an  island group that has fewer people on it
than they do down on St ewart Island, and they have very similar issues to the people of
Stewart Island. You see, people have discove red the Chathams, and increasingly people
are travelling there to visit them. They also have the same problem of a very low rating
base and very little ability to raise funds as  a local authority. They have a high cost for
electricity, very poor roading, a high cost for shipping, and so on.
So when we look at this bill, Mr Roy, I am saying that it is not unique. It is a bill that
could be applied to other parts of New Zeala nd, particularly when they face the issue of
raising enough money to invest in infrastructure. I think that is going to become a whole
lot harder under the local government reforms that we have just had announced by the
Minister a couple of days ago, because with capped rates in areas like the Chathams and
small local authority areas like the West Coas t and others, the abilit y to raise additional
revenue is going to be very difficult indeed. Therefore such  local authorities will be
unable to invest into much-needed infrastructure. The idea of a levy is one that has been
thought of by Southland District Council— good on them. But I would say to the
Government that maybe it is time to listen to the former Minister of Tourism, the
member for West Coast - Tasman, Damien O’Connor, who raised in his second reading
speech that if we are prepared to put a levy or a tax on for Stewart Island, why do we
not consider a levy or a tax on all visitors coming to New Zealand that would then be
shared among councils around New Zealand, pa rticularly those with low rating bases
that are unable to raise enough revenue to put into the infrastructure that they need?
Having said that, Labour supports this bill. We had some concerns about it when it
went to the Local Government and Environment Committee, but most of those concerns
were actually ironed out with a very good se lect committee process. Now, after a lot of
frustration, particularly from the Mayor of Southland District, Frana Cardno, who, when
I read newspaper reports, got quite irate about  the delay in terms of getting this levy
through and the long process of it happening, I k now that it is going to be welcomed by
the people of Southland. I am certainly going to take up the member’s offer, just to
mention his name when I go over to visit Stewart Island. You see, Stewart Island, like
1172 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012
lots of small places in New Zealand, is a popular tourist destination. I think the member
said 19 cruise ships and something like 40,000 vi sitors arrive down in  Stewart Island. I
read somewhere that one small outlet on the island served 400 cups of coffee in just 4
hours. Now, that might not sound like muc h, but when you have a very small rating
base and very small-business people, then it is  difficult for them to be able to provide
everything that might be needed for touris ts coming on to the island, without additional
help from a levy such as this.
We support this bill. I am pleased it is happening for the memb er, but let us not
forget the other communities around New Zealand that have growing numbers of
tourists, low rating bases, and an inability to raise the capital for a lot of infrastructure
that would, in fact, bring even  more jobs and opportunities to their area. I would hope
that Eric Roy will now take up the challeng e of talking to his Cabinet colleagues and
saying what about a visitor levy from those who come into New Zealand that could be
shared across those councils that are providing very good services in their local areas?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I want to congratulate the member of
Parliament Eric Roy on shepherding this lo cal bill, the Southla nd District Council
(Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill, through the House, and add my
voice to the view that Stewart Island is i ndeed unique. I spent a bit of time on Stewart
Island a few years ago. It is a pretty special place.
In the time that I was spending weeks at a time on the island, there were no cruise
ships. There was certainly fishing activity, and it was a very busy place. The pressures
that those cruise ships and th e visitors have brought to St ewart Island have certainly
increased over the years, but the population ha s not significantly increased. Therein lies
the problem of a small co mmunity in a highly desira ble destination funding the
infrastructure for that visitor presence on the island. Yes, of course they get the benefit
of those visitors. Tourism is a wonderful sour ce of income, as is fishing, for the locals
of Stewart Island, but none th e less a very small population  and large visitor numbers
over the years—which are increasing—have meant pressure on the ratepayers of
Stewart Island to fund that necessary infrastructure.
Those of us who represent small comm unities—I can think of, perhaps, the
Mackenzie District Council, for example, wh ich has a small, static rating base and a
desirable destination for visitors—come under th e same sort of pressures, but I have to
acknowledge and agree with my colleague Eric Roy that in the case of Stewart Island,
this is acute. It might well be that the Ch athams are under the same sorts of conditions,
and maybe in time they will also bring a local  bill to the House for our consideration. I
reckon that that probably would also enj oy support from members who understand the
pressures that ratepayers have under these circumstances.
This is a really interesting bill, because it  does what we would not consider doing on
the mainland, if you like, and that is it imposes a levy on visitors. We would not do that
in Ranfurly, because there are many roads in to Ranfurly, and the cost of gathering
that—

items.speaker: Eric Roy
items.text: Hubodometers on your bike trail.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, yes—hubodometers. My coll eague is being particularly
helpful with my speech and he is suggesti ng that hubodometers on the bike trail are an
option—as indeed they are—but the point is there are many roads in and out of
Ranfurly. There are many roads in and out of Ōāmaru, of W ānaka, and of any number
of small visitor destinations in New Zealand, but there are on ly a couple of ways to get
to Stewart Island. You can either get to Stewart Island by boat, or you can arrive on an
aeroplane. I think I prefer the aeroplane. I know it is bumpy, and I know you tend to
wave around a bit, but you can get airsick, or  you can get boat sick. There are two ways
to get to Stewart Island, and so it becomes a little bit easier to collect the levy.
21 Mar 2012 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 1173
I think the provisions in the bill that describe  how that levy is to be utilised are quite
useful. What this bill will do is give the Southland District Council—and that is on
behalf of the Stewart Island community—the legal mechanisms to receive the levy
moneys and also the ability to spend th e levy moneys. I think I read something
around—did I read $16,000? I beg you pardon; $160,000 per annum is projected to be
brought in from that levy. That represents  about 40,000 people going to Stewart Island
each year.
That $160,000 will enable th e local community to upgrade the sewerage system,
water supply, and—I do not know, it will be up to them, obviously—maybe some
walking tracks and footpaths. That is the stu ff of local government, an d that is the stuff
that this local community will be able to  spend the money on. I want acknowledge that
Eric Roy has been working on this issue since 1994, and if you do the maths that is
quite some considerable time to consider—

items.speaker: Eric Roy
items.text: Just after I left school.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Just after he left school, in fact, which has given plenty of time for
the consideration of this bi ll by the wider community and by Parliament. I understand a
number of parliamentarians have also considered this bill.
The powers that this bill gives to the Southland District Council are that it can collect
and spend the levy by establis hing a subcommittee consisti ng of representatives from
the tourism industry, the community board, and the district council. I am assuming that
the community board refers to the Stewart Island Community Board, so it will indeed be
the locals, together with the tourism indus try, who will be the people charged with
spending these fees.
It is interesting that through the course of this bill a number of changes were made to
it at the select committee, and I am interested that new clause 3 was put into the bill. It
clarifies that this levy would not  impact on the locals. It woul d impact on visitors to the
island, so it would not impact on those fish ermen who came and went from the island,
or, indeed, anybody else who had business in I nvercargill. They would not be impacted,
so this is quite tightly focused on where the levy needs to be collected from.
I am very pleased to stand up to speak in the third reading of the Southland District
Council (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill. I want to congratulate,
once again, Eric Roy on doing what a good electorate MP should do, and that is looking
after the interests of his constituents, and with that I commend the bill to the House.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman): I too would like to
stand up and congratulate Eric Roy, the loca l member down there, and to tell him that
he is very, very lucky that he has got  the Southland Distri ct Council (Stewart
Island/Rakiura Visitor Le vy) Empowering Bill going through now, because I am
guessing that under the local government reforms proposed by National none of this
would be allowed. I am not quite sure whethe r tourism infrastructure would be allowed
to be a core part of local government se rvices. So good on you, Mr Roy. I think it is
great that you have done that.
I guess the question is whether, without the reforms, the member who has just
spoken, Jacqui Dean, would be bringing a local bill to the House. I know that her patch,
the Mackenzie District—indeed, one of the smallest in this country—is hosting well
over a million visitors who pass through that area every year, and is actually paying for
toilets, for the provision of water, and for other services for those million-plus people.
In fact, I am not sure of the final figur e; probably 1.5 million people travel through the
Mackenzie Basin. The costs are, as has been acknowledged, a dilemma for many, many
small councils throughout the country.
Can I firstly, though, acknowledge the victims of the terrible tragedy in Foveaux
Strait with the Easy Rider. I understand that the boat had a chequered career. It spent
1174 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012
some time in Westport, which is, indeed, my home town. I think it was a tug or a boat
used around the harbour. It had been altere d—I am not sure whether “upgraded” is the
word. It had been used around the coast of Ne w Zealand for a number of  activities. It is
a very, very sad and tragic situation that we have down in Southland. We hope that the
families and the community can get through their pain and their suffering, and our
hearts go out to them.
Can I come back to this bill, though—and I will not take too long—just to say that it
is a good bill, because it does in fact levy the people who use the services of Stewart
Island, of the national park th ere, and the wonderful facili ties down there at Rakiura.
But the same situation applies, as my co lleague Annette King said, to New Zealand
across the board. We have a number of councils—not just the Chatham Islands Council,
not just the Westland District Council, not just the Mackenzie Di strict Council or the
Kaikōura District Council, but a number of councils—that are burd ened. In fact, the
previous Minister of Local Government said they were unreasonably spending money
on providing promotion and services to t ourists, people who proba bly would be quite
happy to pay for the right services and to support environmental safeguards.
In Government I have always been an advo cate of an environmental levy. It is not a
tax, as such, and it should not be paid when people leave the country; it should be paid
when they come in. They should know they are paying it as part of their airfare, and that
it goes towards environmental infrastructure: to toilets, to signa ge, and to good, smart
investment in infrastructure, such as will happen on Stewart Island under the committee,
I am sure. But that wisdom and that mana gement should be allowed to prevail right
through New Zealand, and ther e should be a fund generated from people coming into
this country, so that we can help and assist  the councils to provide infrastructure that
supports our “100% Pure New Zealand” brand. It is an aspirational brand. We are not
perfect, but for most people in the world we match up to it pretty well. But locals and
people who travel around the country more ofte n than the casual visitor might start to
notice things that we are not doing quite right.
We would like the councils to spend a bit more money. Depending on the outcome of
the proposed local government reforms, I guess they might or might not be allowed to
do that. We hope they will, because it is  a core part of supporting the community,
supporting infrastructure, and generating inco me from tourism and domestic visitors
who come in and out of their districts.
We support the bill. I support the bill. I th ink it is a good move. The alternatives,
unless we have a universal levy across the country on people coming in and out of our
country, are bed taxes, airport taxes, voluntary levies, targeted  rates, and any other sort
of imaginative idea that councillors and pe ople up and down this country have to pay
for the essential things that this levy will pa y for on Stewart Island but also need to be
paid for around the rest of this country. Congratulations, Eric Roy. You have got it
through just in time, and I hope the people down there appreciate that. Kia ora.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: On behalf of the Green Party we extend our
condolences to the families and friends of people on the Easy Rider for their tragic loss.
Co-leader Metiria Turei is attending the tangi of  some of the victims of that accident in
Foveaux Strait, and our good wishes go to th ose families in working through all of the
grief that they are feeling.
The Green Party supports the Southland Di strict Council (Ste wart Island/Rakiura
Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill, and I congr atulate Eric Roy on his leadership in
expanding the revenue sources for the local council to include this levy. I think what we
are seeing with the Government’s pr oposed local government reforms and the
Government’s concern about the rise in rates spending is that instead of looking
constructively with local councils for other potential revenue stre ams, the Government
21 Mar 2012 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 1175
is focusing very much on rates. This bill is  very wise because it is diversifying that
revenue stream.
As other members have pointed out, there is an advantage in having a consistent
nationwide levy similar to the one that is proposed here, so that we do not get a
succession of local bills proposing ad hoc measures by which councils can endeavour to
provide the infrastructure that  our tourists need. We have  had issues in areas like
Damien O’Connor’s electorate, where councils have been una ble to fund dump stations
and the range of public toilets that are needed  for visitors. What this bill does is provide
some funding for that for a small community that has got limited rates funding.
Rather than have an ad hoc series of local bills, I suppor t, as I said in my second
reading speech, a much more nationwide c ontestable fund to which local authorities
could apply to get funding for local governme nt infrastructure in order to service
visitors. It is ironic, I think, that this bill is going forward at the same time that the
Government is looking to constrain the core se rvices of local authorities. I notice in the
bill that some of the funding that the levy w ill generate is to go to the provision of
walking tracks and amenity ar eas close to the national park , and I wonder whether that
sort of function will be considered part of  the core functions of local government under
the changes to the competencies that are be ing proposed to the Local Government Act.
It is that breadth of function that is really important for local authorities.
The Southland District Council has recognised the vital role  that tourists play in
Southland and the national economy, and through th e bill it is seeking to ensure that it
maintains the areas that tourists come to to  visit; that it provides the services that
tourists expect, such as a solid jetty, good walking tracks, and good toilet facilities; and
that it has the ability to fund this. If we have local councils having their competencies
restricted, it does not encourage them to take  a wide look at the ec onomic activities that
can occur in their areas. If they are to be restricted in providing good quality local
infrastructure, does that mean that some of those community development functions that
the Southland District Council is seeking to help fund through this bill will not be able
to be progressed?
We also note that 86 percent of Rakiura / Stewart Island is c onservation land. If we
are going to maintain good infrastructure, we ne ed to maintain the natural infrastructure
as well, because of the ecosystem services  that those wild la nds on Rakiura provide.
That means undertaking good pest control so th at visitors, when they come here, can
enjoy the full diversity of the birdlife, the other wildlife, and the plant communities that
have not been devastated by possums and deer. So instead of cutting the Department of
Conservation’s funding, actually increasing it so  that it can do adequate pest control is
equally important in maintaining the infrastructure on Stewart Island, because those
forested and natural areas are part of that natural infrastructure.
We support the bill, and we encourage Mr Roy to show the leadership he has
provided here to encourage his colleagues to  look at diversifying the revenue streams
for local councils elsewhere in New Zealand to  include a return of the regional fuel tax,
and to recognise the value in councils engaging in all of the competencies that they are
currently able to under the Local Government Ac t 2002. I commend the bill to the
House, and I am pleased to support it. Thank you.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am delighted to take a call on this
local bill, the Southland District Counc il (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy)
Empowering Bill. I want to start by acknowledging Eric Roy. I think what we are seeing
in the House this evening is a fantastic example of a local member of Parliament
working over a long period of time for his c onstituents. I understand that he has been
working since 1994 to try to get what is, I think, access to better services for the people
of Stewart Island and better infrastructure.
1176 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012
Can I also, as has already been acknowledged this evening, send out my thoughts and
prayers to the people of Southland. Obviously  we know that they have been mourning
with the Easy Rider tragedy, and I think all members of this House would be thinking of
the people of Southland at this time.
Can I also acknowledge some comments that Annette King made earlier in the House
this evening. I am fortunate to represent not just the people of central Auckland but also
many islands in the Hauraki Gulf. I represen t Waiheke Island, Great Barrier Island, and
a number of other islands, and some of the issu es that have been raised in this debate,
and also through the passage of this legislation, are applicable to other islands. But what
I would say is that what Mr Roy has done  is win the argument through the select
committee process to get good support for this bill, to say that there are some unique
things about Stewart Island—and I want to t ouch briefly on some of the unique things
about this particular island. He is an exam ple of an MP who has really fought for his
local community in delivering this bill to the House.
Some of the unique things about Stew art Island that I think we should all
acknowledge this evening are that 85 percent of  the island is in a national park. I think
that Rakiura National Park is 10 years ol d now. As has also been mentioned by the
Green Party, we have a numb er of special New Zealand sp ecies on the island, from the
kakapo to the kiwi, so it is a very important  part of the conservation estate for New
Zealand, and I think we can ac knowledge that many people want  to visit the island. In
fact, my understanding is that there are around 40,000 non-residents who visit the island
a year. We estimate that the levy should ra ise about $160,000. I think that is very, very
significant for a small community like the community on Stewart Island.
The other core point that I want to make  today is that the Local Government and
Environment Committee did make a number of changes. We did have that discussion as
to whether this was setting a precedent for other islands within New Zealand and
whether this was a unique situation. I thi nk the select committee process was very
valuable because we did make a number of ch anges. For instance, the new clause 3 to
clarify that a levy could only be applied to visitors travelling to the island and not to all
people travelling to the island was, I think, very significant. We also added a new clause
5—because we obviously heard about implementation issues—to allow the council to
make bylaws to prescribe the rates of levi es and the means of collecting them. We
thought that was very important from an operational perspective. Then we deleted
clauses 6 and 7 and inserted a new clause 6, which I think really was about consistency.
The point that I would make, and it has already been made by Annette King this
evening, is that by passing this legislation I think we are really he lping the people of
Stewart Island to be able to deliver the visito r infrastructure that it is very difficult for
them to be able to pay for. The second th ing we are doing is improving the viability of
the island as a tourism destination. The third thing that I think we are all acknowledging
here this evening is that this is a very good example of a local member doing a very
good job over a significant period of time, advocating for his community, to deliver
some legislation that will ma ke a real difference to a small, isolated community in New
Zealand, and there are many members in th is House who represent communities like
that. I commend this bill to the House a nd I commend Eric Roy for his long advocacy
for the people of Stewart Island. Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First in
support of the Southland District Council (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy)
Empowering Bill; New Zealand First is certainl y in support of this bill. Firstly, I also
endorse the comments of other members in terms of the condolences to the family,
whānau, and friends of those lost in the Easy Rider tragedy. Foveaux Strait, as we all
know, is a very unforgiving piece of water and has had many tragedies in the past also,
21 Mar 2012 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 1177
and this latest tragedy is a great shame a nd a great loss to many in Bluff and Stewart
Island.
I also would like to comment and applaud the local MP, Eric Roy, for carrying this
through over many years. Apparently this issu e goes right back to the 1970s originally,
and the islanders have been asking for the last  three or four decades for assistance. So it
is good to see that this is finally coming to  be. I also acknowledge the chairman of the
Local Government and Environment Committee, Chris Auchinvole, for helping to move
this through. I notice th at the chairman just arrived in the Chamber a short while ago,
obviously in time to hear the adulations that  were going to be bestowed on him. I say
well done to him also for pushing this through.
Stewart Island is only a 1-hour ferry ride from the mainland, from the South Island,
and 15 minutes by air, but it is a community that is very  unique in New Zealand in
terms of being the third-largest island in the New Zealand nation. As a result, with
fewer than 500 people living on the island it has some unique demands and
requirements that many other communities in New Zealand who are not out on an island
limb, out in isolation, in a sense, do not have to put up with.
You can imagine what the impact must be wh en a large cruise sh ip arrives in port
there and several thousand tourists invade wh at is a small community with fewer than
500 people, where there are only 12.8 kilometres  of sealed roads and 8.3 kilometres of
gravel roads, where many of the people liter ally have to walk down the middle of the
road because there are no footpaths, and where the infrastructure is not able to cope with
the tourist numbers that arrive. Over th e summer the New Zealand tourists and
international tourists that arrive on ferries too put a huge amount of pressure on the likes
of the public toilets, on their infrastructure, on their water—they have no reticulated
water—and on the basic utilities on the island.
Of course, we have there the Rakiura National Park, which was opened in 2002,
covering some 157,000 hectares of  land. Eighty-five percent of  Stewart Island is taken
up by that wonderful national park, and having  such a wonderful na tional park brings
with it its own pressures and br ings with it tourists and all sorts of visitors who wish to
see that wonderful piece of native and natural New Zealand bush. Therefore, this is a
good step forward to provide a levy so that visiting tourists and visitors to the island can
help contribute in a relatively small but significant way to some of the costs to assist the
locals.
I applaud the Stewart Island Community Board and also the Southland District
Council for pushing this thr ough and being behind this sc heme. The local community
board has played a pivotal role in bringing th is forward, and it is to  be congratulated as
well on the consultation that it undertook. The board put out something like 485 fliers a
few years ago, received 129 responses, and of those 129 who responded, 119 were in
support of this levy being implemented. That  is a very good result and it shows that
there is strong support for this.
New Zealand First does support local initiatives and local choice by local
communities. We feel that it is up to a lo cal community to determine how they can
assist themselves with funding of this natu re, and we certainly feel this is very
appropriate for an island in a situation like this, where they have very limited ways of
otherwise securing revenue and income to try to cover the costs of the necessary
infrastructure. This is a wise move, with cross-party support, and it is very good that we
all in this House are supporting this initiative; it will greatly assist. The $160,000 on the
face of it does not seem a lot of money, but if  you multiply that over a number of years
and you expand that out, it will increm entally provide a good amount of basic
infrastructure that they do require.
1178 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012
It is ironic that this bill is being put through this week, in terms of what has happened
in local government this week. There have been so many things happening in local
government in New Zealand this week, both go od and bad, and it is  perhaps time that
the members in this House reflect on what  local government means to New Zealand.
We are central government here, but we must remember that much of the services and
much of the infrastructure around New Zeala nd, and much of the community facilities
and the community amenity values that are provided, are provided at local government
level. Certainly, it is ofte n with support from Governme nt and funding support from
Government, but at the end of the day it is our 70 or 80 local authorities around New
Zealand that provide much of the local co mmunity infrastructure, and we must be
mindful of that.
I am very concerned as a former mayor, as  a former councillor, and as a former
community board member about some aspect s of the moves by the Government this
week, in terms of cutting into local government . Certainly there are savings to be made,
certainly there are savings to be had, and certa inly we can be more frugal, as we can in
all areas of life, and I certainly support meas ures to save money, but I certainly do not
support measures that will affect local co mmunities and where local communities could
actually be very adversely affected as a result of some of the proposed cuts by
Government in local governme nt. Therefore, this perhaps is a very timely reminder of
local government being called on to try to put through something that will support their
local communities, and this has been done in this case on Stewart Island by the locals
supporting themselves, standing up for themselv es, and putting their best foot forward
to try to improve their local amenities and their local community services.
We strongly support the bi ll. In terms of New Zealand Firs t, we think this is a great
initiative on behalf of the community—the  community doing something for itself—and
also the central government people working w ith local government to ensure there is a
better outcome for all. It is a great shame if, in this country, we are going to start seeing
increased conflict between local government and central government, because at the end
of the day we are only 4.5 million New Zealanders. We rely on working together to
make this country a better place, and I cer tainly would not like us to start moving down
the track of central government becoming ve ry adversarial towards local government,
because that will not see this country going forward in the future. Thank you.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: It is a great pleasure that I also get to
speak to the Southland District Council (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy)
Empowering Bill. Like everyone else I would li ke to pay tribute to my colleague Eric
Roy. As a new member of the House I can say he has certainly demonstrated to me that
determination and perseverance can definitely achieve results in this House.
I am embarrassed to say that I have not actually visited Stewart Island myself, but, of
course, I have heard many, many st ories of the whitetail, the p āua, and the seafood that
come from Stewart Island. Anothe r thing that I can really iden tify with is the fact that
many of the residents there are direct desc endants of the whaler s and early Rakiura
Māori, with combined family histories reach ing back almost 200 years. Some of the
houses built by the early Norwegian whalers are still lived in today, and their distinctive
alpine architecture somehow is no longer out of place in the roaring forties of the
Southern Ocean. The reason why I can identify w ith this is that I have a community in
my own electorate, at Pūhoi, which was first settled by the Bohemians, and we still have
some of the original families there. The culture and the spirit  of the place can really be
captured only when you have original settlers in a town like that. So I really can identify
with the spirit that is being captured on Stewart Island.
The other thing I would like to mention is the fact that there is consensus in the
House and support in the House for this bill . But there is one member, whom I would
21 Mar 2012 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 1179
like to mention, who has really  put himself on the line in terms of support for Stewart
Island, and that is the H on David Parker. While down on  Stewart Island—and I note
that my colleague Eric Roy was talking about  the challenges associated with roading,
aggregate, getting metals to the island, and, obviously, having to pass over one of our
most difficult stretches of water in the country—Mr Parker was helping with some
roading and some infrastructure. Unfortunately, he got caught on the wrong end of a tar
truck and was covered in tar, but, luckily, it was cold mix tar and not hot mix tar.
I think that one of the big is sues for Stewart Island and its future survival is going to
be based around tourism, because, unfortunately, some of its business has declined over
the years. As Mr Roy mentioned, 17 cruise sh ips arrived last year and this business is
going to continue to grow, hopefully, in the future. But I think that in relation to tourism
the fact is that we are competing globally. There is definitely competition out there.
When tourists are coming down to our beautiful part of the world, they are looking for a
good experience—and they get a good experience. However, part of that is being able to
provide world-class infrastructu re and facilities for them. I think it is very clear that,
because of the small population on Stewart Island, it was too big a burden for a small
population like that to be able to keep invest ing in infrastructure that was experiencing
such a large amount of tourist traffic that is  growing on the island. I think that it is not
only important to preserve our environment, which obviously is critical, but it is also
very, very important to be able  to continue to invest in ou r infrastructure and to provide
world-class facilities.
Like Mr Williams mentioned, on the f ace of it $160,000 annually may not appear
much on the surface, but, in actual fact, to a small population, a small island like
Stewart Island, that is actua lly a significant amount of i nvestment going into their
infrastructure each year and will allow them to maintain that infrastructure for future
growth, and future growth in their tourist industry. Finally, I just want to say that again I
commend Mr Roy for shepherding this bill th rough the House. I want to commend this
bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I am not going to praise Eric Roy. I am
sick and tired of hearing pe ople in this House praise Eric Roy. For goodness’ sake! The
member for Invercargill is simply doing the job that he is paid to do for the good people
of Southland, and he is doing it very well, a nd I do not intend to go along with all this
mushy, cross-party praise of Eric Roy. We have had quite enough of that—we have had
quite enough of that.
I believe that $5, if that is  indeed what visitors to Stewart Island are going to be
required to pay under the Southland District  Council (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor
Levy) Empowering Bill, is a small price to pay. I think that $5 is a small price to pay for
what is a fantastic experience, visiting Stewart Island. I have enjoyed the amber delights
that are served at the South Sea Hotel. I have  sampled the fish and chips at the fish and
chip cart in Oban, and many other delights in Stewart Island. The place is one of the
jewels of our country, and I think that this  bill offers an excellent solution to the
challenge faced by the community in Stew art Island of providing infrastructure like
public loos that are of an acceptable standard for the 30,000-odd people who visit the
island every year.
I am sorry only that Eric Roy did not take  up my offer at the Local Government and
Environment Committee to bring along samples of the Bluff oysters and the venison,
which would have perhaps speeded the bill’s progress through the select committee
even more. Labour supports this bill.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: I rise to speak in favour of the Southland District
Council (Stewart Island/Rakiura Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill. I am bound to say that
1180 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012
I have not had the opportunity yet to visit Stewart Island, an d more is the pity; I would
love to get down there. I have—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What about the Chathams?

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: The closest I have been is Bluff, and I have seen it. I have
not been to the Chatham Islands either. There is a long way I have got to go.
I was not on the Local Government and Environment Committee last year either, but
instinctively I am not generally in favour of new taxes and levies. I think we pay enough
taxes and levies as it is, and I do not share great enthusiasm for giving local government
power—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Miserable.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: —hang on, I have not fini shed yet—and giving local
government the opportunity to raise new taxes, but in this situation the logic does seem
to be reasonably compelling. We have here a situation where there is a very small,
remote community, where a large number of visitors come, up to 40,000 a year, and we
do need to get some basic infrastructure in  place there and find a better way of paying
for it.
I salute Eric Roy for his efforts here. The widespread support that this bill has had in
the House is surely testament to the efforts of Eric Roy and the widespread enthusiasm
that people in the House have for him and his efforts. I remember playing in the
Parliamentary Rugby Team with him in the 1990s, and he—[ Interruption] Well, that is
right. He was galloping around the place, and we played in Southland. He is a very
well-regarded local MP, and this bill, I thi nk, is just a small way in which he can
improve the life and economy of part of his electorate in Stewart Island.
I would like to just draw attention to some  of the details that were handled by the
select committee—amendments to clause 4, for example, on definitions. The provision
of a definition of “approved operator” is inte nded to assist the council to enter into
contracts for transport operators, such as cruise ship operators. The council, then, would
be able to gather revenue from operators on behalf of passengers rather than separately
from each visitor. I think that is a better way of handling the situation.
The committee also recommended replaci ng clause 18 to make offences
infringement offences. The cost to the counc il of prosecuting offences by a visitor as a
summary offence would be substantial, whereas an infringement offences regime would
be more appropriate for the kind of thing that we are dealing with. Unfortunately, if you
introduce a levy, you do have to have some sort of arrangements for dealing with people
who will not pay, and I think that is a simple way of doing it in a relatively cost-
effective way.
It is my expectation that with this bill an d with this levy Stewart Island will be in a
much better place in the next few years to create a warm and inviting environment for
visitors, whose numbers will surely only grow  over the next decade, as more and more
people realise what a wonderful part of the world this is, and what a wonderful place it
is to visit. Now I think we are in a better place because of this bill, so I commend this
bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I support the Southland
District Council (Stewart Island/Rakiu ra Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill and
congratulate the member Eric Roy.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I would like to speak in support of
the Southland District Council (Stewart Is land/Rakiura Visitor Levy) Empowering Bill.
The miraculous thing about it really is that  it has been such a long time coming. We
have heard various members talk about the long  journey for this particular bill. I would
have thought it was a bit of a no-brainer really  that the Stewart Island people should be
21 Mar 2012 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 1181
helped in this way. Four hundred people cannot possible sustain the visitor numbers that
come through there.
Unlike my colleague Paul Goldsmith, I have been to Stewart Island. For somebody
who has been involved in tourism, garden ing, and walking in the New Zealand bush—
my “Cathedrals of Green”—Stewart Island certainly has an enormous amount of
attractions. I felt as a visito r there that it would be appr opriate to contribute in some
way—and what better way than a visitor levy? For 40,000 people visiting at the moment
it would be $160,000, so about $4 a head, which is about the same price as a cup of
coffee. It is not too much to ask, and it w ould make a huge difference to the ability of
those 400 people on Stewart Isla nd to actually put in the so rts of amenities that they
need if they want to please the visitors who go there in their droves already.
The cruise ships have been referred to. It is all very well to have international visitors
going to a place like Stewart Island and taking advantage of the shor t walk tracks that
can be easily managed in an hour or two, but for the people like me, who like to go for a
longer walk, there is a walk that takes 12 days and takes you right around the island. I
think it is one of the few places in New Zealand where you can still do it—

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Have you done it?

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Not the whole thing, but we can add that to the bucket list for
sure.
I think when it comes to unique properties,  Stewart Island has much to commend it.
So too do the outlying islands. We heard Nikki Kaye talking earlier about the islands of
the Hauraki Gulf, and the member for Rongotai talking about the glories of the Chatham
Islands. All of these places have things to commend them.
To me, Stewart Island has unique properties in the sense of its vegetation and its
wildlife. It is pest-free, apart from the odd marauding vis itor, no doubt. It is  a place that
has the ability to show New Z ealand in the way it used to be to people who want to see
it and who want to experience a kind of ecoto urism that I feel will become more and
more popular in years to come. So for the islanders, by virtue of this levy, tourism,
which is a very good source of income already, will be able to generate more income for
the people of Stewart Island and enable them to live there.
As Eric Roy pointed out very carefully, it is a very expensive place to get to. We saw
through the tragedy in Foveaux Strait—an extremely wild st retch of water—that it is
difficult and dangerous and that you need to  make a conscious d ecision to go there.
When you get there it is very expensive infr astructure-wise to set up businesses and to
have cellphones and the other things that we who are living in more built-up areas all
take for granted.
To me, the ability for people on Stewart Island to make a couple of hundred thousand
dollars—and that would tend to grow as peopl e realise and recognise that there is so
much to offer on Stewart Island—would be something that would generate more and
more interest the more people go there, and co me away from it extolling its virtues. So
as a source of income potentially into the future, the levy is perh aps the salvation of
Stewart Island.
As with many small islands it is very difficult to keep young people there. It is very
difficult for an island to provide employment a nd to be able to l ook after itself through
fishing quotas, mineral exploration, forestr y, or any other things—horticulture is not
really a possibility because of the transport and the logistical issu es—so to be able to
generate income from tourism that does not really impact too hard on the tourist I think
is a fantastic idea. Four dollars is not going to  put anyone off visiting. It is really a very
painless levy. In Palmerston North I think you ha ve to pay more than that to get out of
the place, and it is worth every cent. I speak now without any major disloyalty—

items.speaker: Hon David Carter
items.text: It’s always a pleasure to leave.
1182 Southland District Council (Stewart Island) Bill 21 Mar 2012

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: It is always a pleasure to leav e, indeed. Gary McCormick used
to not think so. I spent a year in Palmerst on North—in fact, I lived in Feilding, mostly
because Tom Scott called it the “Athens of th e South Pacific”, and I felt that that was
sufficiently intriguing. For Palmerston Nort h itself the contentious nature of that
departure tax has been well versed, and I wi ll not track through it now , but it is nothing
like the sort of levy we are talking about he re. I think that 245 kilometres of walking

There is talk of the pristine beaches and the sheltered inlets and so forth, so even for

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Oh, leave yourself out of it.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: We talk, of course, about the blue cod, the oysters, and the
salmon, which are not going to be going a nywhere across the House any old time soon,
because clearly some of them do not deserve it. It is very much a place where generosity
